passages.source_text: Ἀναγνοὺς οὖν ὁ Ἰάκωβος τὴν ἐπιστολὴν μετεκαλέσατο τοὺς πρεσβυτέρους, καὶ αὐτοῖς ἀναγνοὺς ἔφη Ἀναγκαίως καὶ πρεπόντως περὶ τῆς ἀληθείας ἀσφαλίζεσθαι ὁ ἡμέτερος ὑπέμνησε Πέτρος, ὅπως τὰς τῶν αὐτοῦ κηρυγμάτων διαπεμφθείσας ἡμῖν βίβλους μηδενὶ μεταδώσωμεν ὡς ἔτυχεν ἢ ἀγαθῷ τινὶ καὶ εὐλαβεῖ, τῷ καὶ διδάσκειν αἱρουμένῳ ἐνπεριτόμῳ τε ὄντι πιστῷ. καὶ ταῦτα μὴ πάντα ὁμοῦ, ἵνα ἐὰν ἐν τοῖς πρώτοις ἀγνώμων φωραθῇ, τὰ δεύτερα μὴ πιστευθῇ. διὸ μὴ ἔλαττον ἔτεσιν ἓξ δοκιμαζέσθω, καὶ εἶθ’ οὕτως κατὰ τὴν Μωϋσέως ἀγωγὴν ἀγαγόντα αὐτὸν ἐπὶ ποταμὸν ἢ πηγὴν (ὅπερ ἐστὶν „ζῶν ὕδωρ“, ἔνθα ἡ τῶν δικαίων γίνεται ἀναγέννησις) μὴ ὁρκίσαι (ἐπεὶ μὴ ἔξεστιν), ἀλλὰ στῆναι αὐτῷ κελεῦσαι πρὸς τῷ ὕδατι καὶ ἐπιμαρτύρασθαι, ὡς καὶ αὐτοὶ ἀναγεννώμενοι κελευσθέντες ἐποιήσαμεν τοῦ μὴ ἁμαρτεῖν χάριν.

λεγέτω δὲ Μάρτυρας ἔχοιμι οὐρανόν, γῆν, ὕδωρ, ἐν οἷς τὰ πάντα περιέχεται, πρὸς τούτοις δ’ ἅπασιν καὶ τὸν διὰ πάντων διήκοντα ἀέρα, οὗ ἄνευ οὐκ ἀναπνέω, ὡς ἀεὶ ὑπήκοος ἔσομαι τῷ τὰς βίβλους μοι τῶν κηρυγμάτων διδόντι, καὶ αὐτάς μου τὰς βίβλους, ἃς ἂν μοι δῷ, οὐ μὴ μεταδῶ τινὶ κατ’ οὐδένα τρόπον, οὐ γράψας, οὐ γεγραμμένον δούς, οὐ γράφοντι ἀναδιδούς, οὐκ αὐτός, οὐ δι’ ἄλλου, οὐ δι’ ἄλλης τινὸς ἀγωγῆς ἢ δόλου ἢ μηχανῆς, ἢ ἀμελῶς φυλάσσων ἢ τιθῶν ἢ νεύων ἢ ἄλλῳ οἱῳδήποτε τρόπῳ ἢ ἐπινοίᾳ ἑτέρῳ αὐτὰ μεταδιδούς. πλὴν ἐὰν δοκιμάσω τινὰ ἄξιον (ὡς αὐτὸς ἐκρίθην ἢ καὶ πλεῖον δοκιμάσας, πλὴν οὐκ ἔλαττον ἔτεσιν ἕξ) τότε εὐλαβεῖ καὶ ἀγαθῷ, διδάσκειν ἐπαναρουμένῳ, ὡς παρέλαβον παραδώσω, καὶ ταῦτα ἐπὶ τῇ τοῦ ἐπισκόπου μου γνώμῃ ποιησάμενος.

ἄλλως δὲ οὐδ’ ἂν τέκνον ἢ ἀδελφὸς ἢ φίλος ἢ ἄλλως πως ποτὲ γένους μοι ἀνήκων, ἐάνπερ ἀνάξιος ᾖ, τοῦδε μὴ μεταδοῦναι χάριν, ὡς οὐ προσῆκεν. οὔτε ἐπιβουλὴν φοβηθήσομαι, οὐ δώροις κολακευθήσομαι. ἀλλ’ εἰ καὶ δόξειέν μοι ποτὲ τὰ διδόμενά μοι τῶν κηρυγμάτων βιβλία μὴ ἀληθῆ εἶναι, οὐδ’ οὕτως μεταδώσω, ἀλλ’ ἀποδώσω. ἀποδημῶν δὲ σὺν ἐμοὶ αὐτὰ κομίσω, ἅπερ ἂν τύχω κεκτημένος· εἰ δὲ μὴ βουληθῶ μεθ’ ἑαυτοῦ αὐτὰ περιφέρειν, ἐπὶ τῆς οἰκίας μου εἶναι αὐτὰ οὐκ ἐάσω, ἀλλὰ τῷ ἐπισκόπῳ μου τῷ τὴν αὐτὴν ἔχοντι πίστιν καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν αὐτῶν ὁρμωμένῳ παρακαταθήσομαι. εἰ δὲ καὶ τύχοι με νοσῆσαι καὶ τὸν θάνατον ὑποπτεύσαι, ἐὰν ἄτεκνος ὦ, ὁμοίως ποιήσω. ἀλλ’ εἰ καὶ τελευτῶ τέκνον ἔχων οὐκ ἄξιον ἢ μηδέπω δυνάμενον, ὁμοίως ποιήσω· τῷ γὰρ ἐπισκόπῳ μου παρακαταθήσομαι·, ἵνα εἰ μὲν τύχοι, ἐφ’ ἡλικίας γενόμενος, ἄξιος εἶναι τῆς πίστεως, ὡς πατρῴαν παρακαταθήκην τῷ τέκνῳ ἀποδώσει, κατὰ τὸν τῆς διαμαρτυρίας λόγον.

ὅτι δὲ οὕτως ποιήσω, πάλιν τὸ δεύτερον διαμαρτύρομαι οὐρανόν, γῆν, ὕδωρ, ἐν οἷς τὰ πάντα περιέχεται, πρὸς τούτοις δ’ ἅπασιν καὶ τὸν διὰ πάντων διήκοντα ἀέρα, οὗ ἄνευ οὐκ ἀναπνέω, ὡς ἀεὶ ὑπήκοος ἔσομαι τῷ τὰς βίβλους μοι τῶν κηρυγμάτων διδόντι καὶ φυλάξω κατὰ πάντα ὅσα διεμαρτυράμην ἢ καί τι πλεῖον. φυλάσσοντι οὖν μοι τὰς συνθήκας μέρος ἔσται μετὰ τῶν ὁσίων, ποιήσαντι δὲ παρ’ ἃ συνεθέμην, ἐχθρὸν εἴη μοι τὸ πᾶν καὶ ὁ διὰ πάντων διήκων αἰθὴρ καὶ ὁ ὑπὲρ τὰ ὅλα θεός, οὗ κρείττων, οὗ μείζων οὐδείς. ἀλλ’ εἰ καὶ εἰς ἑτέρου θεοῦ ὑπόνοιαν γένωμαι, κἀκεῖνον νῦν ὄμνυμι ὡς οὐκ ἄλλως ποιήσω, εἴτ’ ἔστιν εἴτ’ οὐκ ἔστιν. πρὸς τούτοις δ’ ἅπασιν εἰ ψεύσομαι, κατάθεμα ἔσομαι ζῶν καὶ θανὼν καὶ αἰωνίῳ κολασθήσομαι κολάσει. καὶ μετὰ τοῦτο ἄρτου καὶ ἅλατος μετὰ τοῦ παραδιδόντος μεταλαβέτω.

ταῦτα τοῦ Ἰακώβου εἰπόντος ὠχρίασαν ἀγωνιάσαντες οἱ πρεσβύτεροι. συνιδὼν οὖν ὁ Ἰάκωβος ὅτι λίαν πεφόβηνται, ἔφη Ἀκούσατέ μου, ἀδελφοὶ καὶ σύνδουλοι. ἐὰν τὰς βίβλους πᾶσιν ὡς ἔτυχεν παράσχωμεν καὶ· αὗται ὑπὸ τολμηρῶν ἀνδρῶν τινῶν νοθευθῶσιν ἢ ταῖς ἑρμηνείαις διαστραφῶσιν, ὡς ἤδη τινὰς ἠκούσατε πεποιηκότας, ἔσται λοιπὸν καὶ τοῖς ὄντως τὴν ἀλήθειαν ζητοῦσιν ἀεὶ πλανᾶσθαι. διὸ ἄμεινον παρ’ ἡμῖν αὐτὰς εἶναι καὶ μεταδιδόναι μετὰ πάσης τῆς προειρημένης ἀσφαλείας τοῖς θέλουσι ζῆν εὐσεβῶς καὶ ἄλλους σῴζειν. εἰ δέ τις μετὰ τὸ οὕτως διαμαρτύρασθαι ἄλλως ποιήσει, εὐλόγως αἰωνίᾳ ὑποπεσεῖται κολάσει. τίνι γὰρ λόγῳ ἄλλων ἀπωλείας αἴτιος γενόμενος αὐτὸς οὐκ ἀπολεῖται; τῶν οὖν πρεσβυτέρων ἐπὶ τῇ τοῦ Ἰακώβου γνώμῃ ἡσθέντων καὶ εἰπόντων Εὐλόγηται ὁ σὲ ὡς πάντα προειδὼς καλῶς ἡμῖν καταστήσας ἐπίσκοπον — καὶ ταῦτα εἰπόντων αὐτῶν ἐγερθέντες προσηυξάμεθα τῷ τῶν ὅλων πατρὶ καὶ θεῷ· „ᾧ ἡ δόξα εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας. ἀμήν“.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.

passages.text: After James had read the letter, he summoned the elders, and after reading it to them he said, “Necessarily and fittingly, our Peter has reminded us to take precautions concerning the truth, so that we should not pass on indiscriminately to anyone the books of his proclamations that have been sent to us, but only to someone good and devout, one who chooses to teach and is a circumcised believer. And we should not pass on all of them at once, so that if he is discovered to be untrustworthy with the first, he will not be entrusted with the later ones. Therefore, let him be tested for no fewer than six years. Then, after bringing him in accordance with the way of Moses to a river or a spring—which is ‘living water,’ where the rebirth of the righteous takes place—do not make him swear an oath, since that is not permitted. Instead, command him to stand beside the water and make a solemn attestation, just as we ourselves did when we were commanded to do so as we were being reborn, for the sake of not sinning.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: indiscriminately
lexical_decisions.rationale: The idiom means without careful selection, rather than merely by chance.

lexical_decisions.chosen: is a circumcised believer
lexical_decisions.rationale: Takes ἐνπεριτόμῳ adjectivally of the qualified recipient without altering the supplied form.

lexical_decisions.chosen: untrustworthy
lexical_decisions.rationale: In the context of testing a recipient’s handling of restricted books, this conveys deficient judgment or reliability better than the narrower ‘ungrateful.’

lexical_decisions.chosen: in accordance with the way of Moses
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀγωγή denotes a prescribed way, discipline, or practice here.

lexical_decisions.chosen: make a solemn attestation
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb introduces the formal invocation of witnesses stated in the following passage without making the act an oath.

passages.text: And let him say: “May I have as witnesses heaven, earth, and water, in which all things are contained, and besides all these also the air that permeates everything, without which I do not breathe, that I will always be obedient to the one who gives me the books of the proclamations, and that, as for my books themselves, whichever he may give me, I will certainly not pass them on to anyone in any way: not by writing them out, not by giving away what has been written, not by handing them over to someone who is writing; not myself, not through another person, not through any other course of action or deception or device; not by guarding them carelessly, or leaving them somewhere, or giving a signal, or by any other method or scheme passing them on to someone else. The only exception is if I test someone and find him worthy—as I myself was judged, or after testing him even more extensively, though for no fewer than six years. Then I will hand them on, just as I received them, to a devout and good person who will undertake to teach, and I will do this with the approval of my bishop.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτάς μου τὰς βίβλους, ἃς ἂν μοι δῷ
lexical_decisions.chosen: as for my books themselves, whichever he may give me
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves both the possessive μου and the emphasis of αὐτάς, while ἃς ἂν is represented by the open-ended ‘whichever.’

lexical_decisions.chosen: I will certainly not pass them on
lexical_decisions.rationale: The paired negatives emphatically deny any future disclosure.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ γράψας, οὐ γεγραμμένον δούς, οὐ γράφοντι ἀναδιδούς
lexical_decisions.chosen: not by writing them out, not by giving away what has been written, not by handing them over to someone who is writing
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the three distinct prohibited routes of copying, distributing written material, and supplying it to a copyist.

lexical_decisions.chosen: or leaving them somewhere, or giving a signal
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the terse actions without specifying an unstated recipient or purpose.

lexical_decisions.chosen: after testing him even more extensively
lexical_decisions.rationale: πλεῖον may concern greater duration or rigor; ‘more extensively’ leaves that dimension open.

lexical_decisions.chosen: who will undertake to teach
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied form is analyzed as a future-middle participle of ἐπαναίρω. In context it prospectively describes taking up or undertaking the work of teaching.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὶ τῇ τοῦ ἐπισκόπου μου γνώμῃ
lexical_decisions.chosen: with the approval of my bishop
lexical_decisions.rationale: γνώμη here denotes the bishop’s judgment or consent governing the transfer.

passages.text: “Otherwise, not even a child or a brother or a friend or anyone in any other way ever related to me, if indeed he is unworthy—for this one’s sake not to pass it on, since it is not proper. I will not fear a plot, nor will I be won over by gifts. But even if at some point the books of the proclamations given to me seem to me not to be true, not even then will I pass them on; instead, I will return them. When traveling, I will carry with me whichever of them I happen to possess. But if I do not wish to carry them about with me, I will not leave them in my house; instead, I will entrust them for safekeeping to my bishop, who holds the same faith and proceeds from the same starting points. If I should also happen to become ill and anticipate death, if I am childless, I will do likewise. But even if I die leaving a child who is unworthy or not yet capable, I will do likewise, for I will entrust them for safekeeping to my bishop, so that if the child, after reaching maturity, should happen to be worthy of the faith, the bishop will return them to the child as a paternal deposit, in accordance with the terms of the solemn attestation.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: Otherwise, not even a child or a brother or a friend or anyone in any other way ever related to me, if indeed he is unworthy—for this one’s sake not to pass it on, since it is not proper
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering remains formally fragmentary rather than supplying an unattested governing verb. It provisionally groups τοῦδε with χάριν as ‘for this one’s sake,’ while the unresolved syntax and alternative reference of τοῦδε remain disclosed in source_issues.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I will not fear a plot
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπιβουλή denotes a hostile design or plot rather than fear in general.

lexical_decisions.chosen: when traveling
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle describes being away on a journey without specifying a particular destination.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰ δὲ μὴ βουληθῶ μεθ’ ἑαυτοῦ αὐτὰ περιφέρειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: if I do not wish to carry them about with me
lexical_decisions.rationale: The reflexive ἑαυτοῦ is understood contextually with the first-person subject; this usage does not require alteration to ἐμαυτοῦ.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I will entrust them for safekeeping
lexical_decisions.rationale: The middle verb describes depositing property with another person as a trust.

lexical_decisions.chosen: proceeds from the same starting points
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the source’s metaphor of setting out from shared principles.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to be worthy of the faith
lexical_decisions.rationale: πίστις most naturally denotes the shared faith in this ecclesial context, though ‘trust’ remains semantically possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a paternal deposit
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the legal image of property entrusted for later restoration as something received from the child’s father.

source_issues.source_quote: ἄλλως δὲ οὐδ’ ἂν τέκνον ἢ ἀδελφὸς ἢ φίλος ἢ ἄλλως πως ποτὲ γένους μοι ἀνήκων, ἐάνπερ ἀνάξιος ᾖ, τοῦδε μὴ μεταδοῦναι χάριν, ὡς οὐ προσῆκεν
source_issues.issue: The construction lacks a securely identifiable governing predicate for the nominative persons and does not establish a clear relation among τοῦδε, μὴ μεταδοῦναι, and χάριν. The translation provisionally takes τοῦδε with χάριν as referring to the unworthy person, but τοῦδε could instead refer to what is transmitted, and other regroupings remain possible. No complete English reconstruction is secure without supplying or reassigning syntax.

source_issues.source_quote: εἰ δὲ μὴ βουληθῶ μεθ’ ἑαυτοῦ αὐτὰ περιφέρειν
source_issues.issue: The reflexive ἑαυτοῦ has a first-person referent supplied by βουληθῶ and the surrounding first-person discourse. This is treated as a possible reflexive usage, not as evidence of textual corruption.
The selected edition prints a middle dot immediately followed by a comma. This is an editorial punctuation anomaly and does not affect the clause’s meaning.

passages.text: “As assurance that I will do so, I once again, for a second time, call as witnesses heaven, earth, and water, in which all things are contained, and besides all these also the air that permeates everything, without which I do not breathe, that I will always be obedient to the one who gives me the books of the proclamations, and I will observe in every respect everything I solemnly attested, or even something more. Therefore, if I keep the agreements, I will have a share with the holy ones; but if I act contrary to what I agreed, may the whole universe be hostile to me, as well as the ether that permeates everything and the God who is above all, than whom no one is better, than whom no one is greater. But even if I come to entertain the supposition of another god, I now swear by that one too that I will not act otherwise, whether he exists or does not exist. Besides all this, if I lie, I will be accursed while alive and after death, and I will be punished with eternal punishment.” After this, let him partake of bread and salt with the one who hands the books on.

lexical_decisions.chosen: once again, for a second time
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the source’s emphatic repetition rather than reducing it to a single temporal expression.

lexical_decisions.chosen: or even something more
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the unqualified additional undertaking without introducing an uncertainty marker.

lexical_decisions.chosen: if I keep the agreements
lexical_decisions.rationale: συνθῆκαι are the solemnly accepted terms or agreements established by the attestation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the ether that permeates everything
lexical_decisions.rationale: Renders αἰθήρ distinctly from the earlier ἀήρ, ‘air,’ while preserving the image of permeation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: if I come to entertain the supposition of another god
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπόνοια can denote supposition or suspicion; the rendering leaves the precise epistemic force open while preserving the hypothetical claim.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I now swear by that one too
lexical_decisions.rationale: The accusative with ὄμνυμι identifies the additional being invoked in the declaration.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I will be accursed while alive and after death
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves ἔσομαι as a future assertion and distinguishes it from the preceding optative εἴη, while representing the contrast between living and having died.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I will be punished with eternal punishment
lexical_decisions.rationale: The future indicative is retained as an asserted consequence rather than recast as a wish.

passages.text: After James said these things, the elders turned pale with anguish. Seeing that they had become very afraid, James said, “Listen to me, brothers and fellow servants. If we make the books available to everyone indiscriminately and they are adulterated by certain daring men or distorted by interpretations, as you have already heard that some have done, the result will be that even those who truly seek the truth will thereafter continually go astray. Therefore, it is better for the books to remain with us and for us to pass them on, with every safeguard previously mentioned, to those who wish to live devoutly and save others. But if anyone, after making such a solemn attestation, acts otherwise, he will justly fall under eternal punishment. For on what grounds will someone who has become responsible for the destruction of others not himself be destroyed?” The elders were pleased with James’s judgment and said, “Blessed is the one who, foreknowing all things, appointed you well as bishop for us.” And when they had said these things, we rose and prayed to the Father and God of all: “To whom is the glory throughout the ages. Amen.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: turned pale with anguish
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves both their visible pallor and the distress that caused it.

lexical_decisions.chosen: are adulterated
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb depicts the books as corrupted by the introduction of spurious material.

lexical_decisions.chosen: distorted by interpretations
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves both the interpretive means and the resulting distortion; ἑρμηνεῖαι may also encompass explanatory renderings or translations.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἔσται λοιπὸν καὶ τοῖς ὄντως τὴν ἀλήθειαν ζητοῦσιν ἀεὶ πλανᾶσθαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: the result will be that even those who truly seek the truth will thereafter continually go astray
lexical_decisions.rationale: Expresses the impersonal construction while retaining λοιπὸν and the continuing force of ἀεί.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he will justly fall under eternal punishment
lexical_decisions.rationale: εὐλόγως marks the punishment as warranted or reasonable, not as verbal praise.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Εὐλόγηται ὁ σὲ ὡς πάντα προειδὼς καλῶς ἡμῖν καταστήσας ἐπίσκοπον
lexical_decisions.chosen: Blessed is the one who, foreknowing all things, appointed you well as bishop for us
lexical_decisions.rationale: Εὐλόγηται is rendered as a perfect passive assertion of a resulting blessed state, not as a wish. The foreknowledge describes the one who made the appointment, and καλῶς evaluates that appointment.

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
